query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The degradation of the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy exhibits a threshold behavior with respect to oxygen partial pressure; above a critical oxygen level, synergistic oxidation among alloying elements leads to formation of a continuous, protective layered oxide scale, whereas at low oxygen partial pressures (or under reducing conditions), incomplete oxidation produces porous, non-protective scales that accelerate degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy featuring a homogeneous FCC matrix confirmed by pre-test compositional analysis.
generation.intervention: Expose samples to a series of oxidation tests at 900 °C for 100 hours with systematically varied oxygen partial pressures (e.g., 1, 5, 10, 50, and 100 mbar).
generation.conditions: Temperature of 900 °C with an oxidation duration of 100 hours; oxygen partial pressures varied from 1 to 100 mbar.
generation.structural_mediator: A transition in oxide scale morphology from porous/non-protective to a continuous, multilayered structure as a function of oxygen availability.
generation.mechanism: The oxidation rate and resultant oxide structure are highly sensitive to available oxygen; above a critical oxygen partial pressure, synergistic interactions among Al, Cr, and Ti promote a continuous protective scale formation. Below this threshold, oxidation is incomplete, leading to porous, poorly adherent oxide scales.
generation.predicted_outcome: A distinct transition in oxidation kinetics and oxide morphology is expected at a marked oxygen partial pressure (e.g., around 10 mbar); samples at or above this threshold will show lower mass gain and a well-developed protective oxide scale, whereas samples below this threshold will show significantly higher mass gain and porous oxide layers.
generation.baseline: Standard oxidation behavior at approximately 10 mbar oxygen partial pressure as typically observed in laboratory settings.
generation.boundary: Test conditions fixed at 900 °C for 100 hours with oxygen partial pressures spanning 1 to 100 mbar.
generation.uncertainty: The exact oxygen partial pressure threshold may vary due to microstructural or local gas composition variations, yet a clear trend should emerge with careful calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a series of oxidation tests at 900 °C for 100 hours while varying oxygen partial pressures (e.g., 1, 5, 10, 50, 100 mbar). Characterize the oxide scale using SEM/TEM and quantify mass gain and porosity.
measurements: Mass gain as a function of oxygen partial pressure
SEM/TEM imaging for oxide scale morphology
Porosity quantification within the oxide layers
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxidation kinetics and oxide morphology vary continuously without a clear transition at a threshold oxygen partial pressure, then the hypothesis of a threshold-driven synergistic effect is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Stochastic CA is used for modeling the oxidation of compositionally complex alloys, as it can reproduce both the thermodynamics and kinetics of oxidation, together with the relevant microstructures []. Being a mesoscale model, CA provides flexibility to import data from lower-length-scale models, which are essential for capturing the effect of oxidation in full. We varied the size of the simulation cell from 50 × 50 to 200 × 200. It was found that the 100 × 50 matrix size is spatially large enough to capture the oxidation processes of interest, in general, and adding more cells only increases computational time, with no next effect on simulated results. Wherever we have used experimental micrographs to model the process, we have modified the simulation cell size to match the aspect ratios of the micrographs. The model adopted in this work was built closely upon our previous efforts of modeling the oxidation behavior of NiAl and Hf-doped NiAl and is explained in detail elsewhere [] (Figure 2 of Reference [] shows a clear flowchart of the model). In this study, we extended the same model for a five-element alloy system. The oxidation reaction with pure metal is assumed to be instanta

From this study, we conclude the following: the oxide scale in HEAs is a function of their complex chemistries and microstructures. We addressed the problem piecewise, studying the oxidation of a single crystal HEA without the microstructural complications and defects to understand the role of alloy chemistry. Subsequently, we considered numerous microstructural features, including compositional segregations observed experimentally, to understand the scale growth in different microstructural regions. We have not yet addressed the problem of internal oxidation using CA. Our future efforts will focus on understanding internal oxidation and subsequently integrate the individual simulations for modeling the microstructures of oxidized HEAs.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding of speciated oxide growth in high entropy alloys.
papers.system: Equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy with modifications (e.g., additional Al)
papers.approach: In situ experiments using atom probe tomography (APT), transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) under controlled low‐temperature oxidation (e.g., 400 °C under 10 mbar O₂) to monitor early-stage layer formation.
papers.findings: Observed rapid formation of compositional oxide layers: an initial Ni-enriched pre-oxide layer, followed by a Cr2O₃ layer, and then a multi-oxide layer rich in Fe, Co, and Mn. With the addition of Al, an extra inner oxide layer is observed along with modified interactions among elements.
papers.mechanism: Proposes that the oxidation process is controlled by a selective speciation process dictated by competitive oxidation kinetics that depend on the standard reduction potentials, atomic size, and cohesive energy density. Al oxidizes rapidly forming an early oxide that perturbs diffusion of other elements.

papers.title: Unraveling the Superior High-Temperature Oxidation Behavior of FeNiCuAl-Based High-Entropy Alloys: Roles of Cr, Co, and Mn Alloying Additions.
papers.system: FeNiCuAl-based high-entropy alloy designed with additional Cr, Co, and Mn, processed via laser cladding with induced nanocrystallinity and trace Y addition
papers.approach: Integration of compositional and microstructural engineering (laser cladding, nanocrystalline microstructure, and trace Y modification) coupled with thermal cycling tests at 900–1000 °C.
papers.findings: Formation of a multilayered oxide scale was achieved with an outer MnCr₂O₄ layer and an inner continuous Al₂O₃ scale, leading to significant reduction in oxide growth rate (up to three orders of magnitude reduction with trace Y) and enhanced spallation resistance under thermal cycling.
papers.mechanism: Synergistic elemental effects produce protective oxides via both thermodynamic stability (Al₂O₃/Cr₂O₃ formation) and kinetic benefits through grain-boundary diffusion (from laser cladding), with the reactive element effect of Y reinforcing the oxide/alloy interface.

papers.title: Enhanced Oxidation Resistance of Ultrafine-Grain Microstructure AlCoCrFeNi High Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with an FCC matrix, processed to achieve an ultrafine-grain microstructure
papers.approach: Severe surface deformation (stationary friction processing at different rpm) to produce refined grain structures, followed by isothermal oxidation tests in the range 850–1050 °C.
papers.findings: Ultrafine-grained samples showed reduced oxidation kinetics (12–48% slower mass gain) compared to as-cast counterparts, with a consistent formation of protective scales (chromia and alumina) and enhanced elemental homogenization.
papers.mechanism: Refined microstructure increases grain-boundary density providing short-circuit diffusion paths that facilitate the formation of a uniform, adherent protective oxide scale without altering the underlying chemical passivation, thus preserving the alloy’s strength and fatigue performance.

papers.title: Modeling Oxidation of AlCoCrFeNi High-Entropy Alloy Using Stochastic Cellular Automata.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with attention to single-crystal and phase-separated microstructures
papers.approach: Stochastic cellular automata (CA) model that integrates thermodynamics, kinetics, and microstructure by incorporating diffusion coefficients from molecular simulations and experimental micrographs.
papers.findings: Simulations reproduced layered oxidation behavior with formation of passivating α-Al₂O₃ and Cr₂O₃ scales. The model predicts that as the alloy’s microstructural complexity increases (segregation, phase separation), the oxide scale may segregate spatially, affecting overall oxidation kinetics.
papers.mechanism: The model elucidates the competition between elemental oxidation tendencies — where fast oxidizers (Al, Cr) form protective oxides and slower oxidizers (Fe, Co, Ni) initially form non-protective oxides that eventually diminish with time — highlighting the importance of chemistry–microstructure interplay in dictating degradation.

established: Oxidation in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) is governed by a complex interplay of elemental chemistry and microstructure.
Protective oxide scales typically form as layered structures with inner alumina/ chromia and outer spinel phases.
Microstructural refinement (e.g., ultrafine grains, enhanced grain boundaries) can improve oxidation resistance by facilitating uniform diffusion and scale formation.

directions.direction: Selective oxide layer formation via reactive element kinetics
directions.assessment: This approach probes how rapid oxidation of elements (such as Al) drives a layered oxide formation that can protect the substrate. It directly addresses the issue of synergistic elemental interactions without altering the FCC matrix and is supported by detailed studies showing early Al‐oxide formation and subsequent layer development (e.g., PMC11169556::web::016, PMC13208696::web::025). It is experimentally feasible using controlled atmosphere exposures and cross‐sectional analytical techniques.

directions.direction: Residual stress and grain-boundary diffusion mediating oxidation
directions.assessment: This direction investigates the role of additive manufacturing–induced residual stresses and high grain-boundary densities, which may accelerate oxidation via fast diffusion pathways. It is relevant since formability and strength must be preserved, and controlled stress-relief treatments can be implemented. Supporting evidence comes from studies on ultrafine-grain oxidation (PMC9026100::web::004) and discussions of AM-induced microstructural features.

directions.direction: Competitive diffusion and elemental segregation effects (e.g. Ti accumulation)
directions.assessment: This approach focuses on how differences in elemental diffusivities—especially the slower diffusion of Ti versus fast oxidizers such as Al and Cr—lead to selective segregation at the metal/oxide interface. Such segregation may enhance scale adhesion and retard spallation. It is directly tied to the elemental kinetic competition observed in similar HEA systems (PMC11169556::web::019, PMC13208696::web::025) and can be explored with high-resolution techniques like APT and TEM-EDS.

directions.direction: Oxygen partial pressure threshold effects on synergistic oxidation kinetics
directions.assessment: This direction examines how varying the oxygen partial pressure modulates the oxidation mechanisms. A threshold behavior is expected such that above a critical O₂ partial pressure, a protective layered oxide forms, whereas under reducing or low-oxygen conditions, the incomplete oxidation leads to porous, non-protective scales. This idea is well grounded in thermodynamic and kinetic models (PMC9498035::web::006) and is eminently testable in controlled gas environments.

directions.direction: Combinatorial compositional modifications under controlled processing
directions.assessment: Altering minor alloying content to decouple synergistic elemental effects can provide insight but may risk altering the FCC matrix and formability. Although conceptually interesting, this approach is less directly aligned with the constraints of preserving the baseline mechanical integrity, making it less promising in the current context.

candidates.changes: Expanded discussion on oxygen partial pressure control and provided deeper details on factors that influence the critical threshold. The design now explicitly outlines how to control and measure oxygen partial pressure and references comparable studies for threshold determination.

candidates.hypothesis: The as-built additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy exhibits accelerated degradation at elevated temperatures due to high residual stresses and abundant grain-boundary diffusion paths, whereas stress-relieved (annealed) samples will display reduced oxidation kinetics and lower mass gain, indicating that AM-induced residual stresses dominate oxidation behavior.
candidates.intervention: Apply a stress-relief annealing treatment (e.g., 600 °C for 2 hours) to a subset of samples prior to oxidation exposure.
candidates.changes: Revised the mechanism and predicted outcome to remove the logical contradiction. The hypothesis now asserts that AM-induced residual stresses and increased grain-boundary density in as-built samples accelerate oxidation due to enhanced diffusion channels, leading to higher mass gain and more spallation compared to stress-relieved (annealed) samples.

candidates.hypothesis: The degradation of the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy is moderated by competitive diffusion processes in which fast-oxidizing elements (Al and Cr) form protective oxides while slower-diffusing Ti accumulates at the metal–oxide interface to act as an anchoring agent that improves scale adhesion and retards spallation; this mechanism is most relevant under oxidizing conditions but becomes less pronounced under reducing environments.
candidates.intervention: Expose samples to an oxidizing environment at 900 °C for 100 hours and, in parallel, conduct tests under reducing gas conditions to compare mechanisms.
candidates.changes: Expanded the hypothesis to acknowledge that the proposed Ti segregation mechanism predominantly applies under oxidizing conditions. Clarified the interactions between Ti and other alloying elements and mentioned that under reducing conditions, diminished oxide formation would lessen the impact of Ti segregation on scale adhesion.

major_issues: Does not address possible synergistic effects of alloy composition even though references emphasize composition-dependent oxidation.
Does not consider the behavior under reducing conditions, contrary to the question asking about both oxidizing and reducing gas environments.
minor_issues: Unclear if the proposed stress-relief step affects mechanical properties or phase stability.
fixes: Incorporate parallel measurements of residual stress, microstructure, and oxide scale composition to clarify synergy with compositional effects.
Explicitly compare oxidation behavior under reducing conditions to determine the role of residual stress in non-oxidizing atmospheres.
evidence_needs: Data on residual stress measurements in as-built vs. annealed samples to confirm the hypothesized effect on oxidation rate.
Prior studies linking stress fields to enhanced diffusivity in additively manufactured high-entropy alloys.

major_issues: Ignores reducing conditions despite the question specifying them, so does not capture the full range of possible degradation pathways.
minor_issues: Limited discussion of potential mechanical or microstructural changes from oxide formation.
fixes: Extend the hypothesis to include a parallel test or rationale for behavior in low-oxygen or reducing atmospheres.
Clarify how the proposed oxide layering might influence mechanical integrity and fatigue performance over time.
evidence_needs: Experimental confirmation that a continuous Al2O3 layer forms in the given composition under the stated conditions.
Comparative oxidation kinetics under different oxygen partial pressures or reducing environments to validate the layered-oxide premise.

minor_issues: May need further clarity on how the slowed diffusion of Ti interacts with other elements (e.g., Ni or Co) in shaping oxide stability.
Does not explicitly note potential repercussions for mechanical properties once Ti segregates at interfaces.
fixes: Examine the interplay of Ti with other elements (especially Ni, Co) to confirm if other second-phase formation or new phases appear during exposure.
Include mechanical testing post-exposure to verify that scale adhesion correlates with improved structural integrity.
evidence_needs: Atom probe tomography or high-resolution TEM to confirm localized Ti segregation at the metal–oxide interface.
Comparison data on scale spallation and adhesion measurements under both oxidizing and reducing conditions.

fixes: Expand the hypothesis to describe or test scale evolution under low-oxygen or reducing conditions to compare and contrast mechanisms.

fixes: Examine potential gradients or transitions in oxide growth behavior instead of a single sharp threshold, possibly by sampling more finely spaced partial pressures.
